label: dochirakatoieba
title_raw: どちらかといえば [どちらかといえば] (dochirakatoieba)
title: どちらかといえば

examples.japanese: どちらかと言えば海に行きたい。
examples.body_text:
どちらかと言えば海に行きたい。 

If I had my druthers, 
		I would like to go to the sea.
examples.body_html:
どちらかと言えば海に行きたい。 
If I had my druthers, I would like to go to the sea.

examples.japanese: どちらかといえば泳ぎはうまい方でした。
examples.body_text:
どちらかといえば泳ぎはうまい方でした。 

		He was, 
		if anything, 
		a good swimmer.
examples.body_html:
どちらかといえば泳ぎはうまい方でした。 
He was, if anything, a good swimmer.

examples.japanese: どちらかといえば今日はあの人に会いたくない。
examples.body_text:
どちらかといえば今日はあの人に会いたくない。 

		I would 
		rather 
		not see him(her) today.
examples.body_html:
どちらかといえば今日はあの人に会いたくない。 
I would rather not see him(her) today.

comments.text: You can also use どちらかというと interchangeably.
comments.html: You can also use どちらかというと interchangeably.

comments.text:
Bamboo4, please excuse my ignorance - I'm a brit and I only found out the meaning of "druthers" in the The American Heritage Dictionary as a slang term for "would rather" from the 1800s.



Can anyone suggest a less esoteric translation for どちらかと言えば - "If it's all the same" or "above all else" ????

comments.text:
I suppose you could say, "If I had to say (one way or the other)" or "If I were to say..."



As in, one way or the other.



どちらかと言えば、彼女が作ったケーキはちょっと・・・

If I say which way is, she-made cake is a little...



"If I had to say one way or the other, the cake she made is a little..."



I think we use this sort of construction in English, too. We say, "If I had to say..." and then state an opinion or observation.



In the case of stating one's desire (If I had my druthers, I'd like to go to the beach) maybe we would say "If I may say..." or something of this nature.



Just my two cents.
